tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Verify causality of an LTI system by checking that its impulse response satisfies $h(t)=0 for all t<0 in the pole-based stability setting$.

blocks.text: A continuous-time LTI system is causal exactly when its impulse response has no active values for negative time, so causality is the rule $h(t)=0$ for every $t<0$. In short: if $h(t)$ is nonzero before $t=0$, the system would require future input values and is noncausal.

The same rule is about support. A right-sided impulse response like $h(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and possibly nonzero for $t\ge 0$ is causal. A left-sided response has support only in $t<0$ and is noncausal. A bilateral response has nonzero values on both sides of the origin and is also noncausal because of the negative-time component.

In this module, we also use the same time-domain rule before pole-based arguments: pole-location checks assume the system passes the causality prerequisite. So first verify the support condition on $h(t)$, and only then move to pole placement for the stability step.

Use stable notation for quick checks from formulas: write the time-domain support statement, check the sign of $t$, and test a representative negative time sample. For the base case $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, use the same rule: since $u(t)=0$ for $t<0$, the impulse response is causal and has no nonzero left-time contribution.

sections.section_title: Checking $h(t)=0 for t<0 from an Impulse Response Formula$

example_content.example_prompt: Check causality of $h(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)-5u(t+2)$ by testing the value of $h(t)$ for $t<0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is whether any part of the impulse response is nonzero for negative time. Use the same rule as the tutorial: a continuous-time LTI system is causal only if $h(t)=0$ for every $t<0$.
Use the step-function support conditions: $u(t)=0$ for $t<0$, and $u(t+2)=0$ for $t<-2$, so the first term is zero on negative time and the second term is only constrained to zero before $t=-2$.

Now test the negative-time region with a representative value, for example $t=-1\in(-2,0)$: the first term has $u(-1)=0$, so $3e^{-(-1)}u(-1)=0$, while the second term has $u(1)=1$, so $-5u(-1+2)=-5$.
Because there exists a negative-time value with nonzero output, $h(t)$ violates the support condition, so this LTI system is noncausal.

sections.section_title: Checking Causality from an Impulse Response Graph

image_slots.image_description: Graph of $h(t)$ versus t. Show clear t-axis and $h(t)$-axis labels, one short nonzero pulse in negative time near $t=-0$.5 to $t=-0$.25, an exponential-looking tail for $t\ge0$, and zero response for all sufficiently small and moderate negative times between pulses and the tail.

example_content.example_prompt: From the graph of $h(t)$ shown, identify whether the LTI system is causal and explain the negative-time support test used.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same causality rule from the tutorial: a continuous-time LTI system is causal only if its impulse response is zero for every negative-time value. So classify by reading support from the graph.

Locate support intervals in the plotted response. Here the graph has nonzero values both around the small negative interval $( -0.5, -0.25 )$ and for $t\ge 0$, so the support is split across negative and nonnegative time.
Now check the negative-time rule directly. Pick one point in the left-side pulse, for example $t=-0.4$, and read $h(-0.4)\neq 0$ from the graph.

Because at least one nonzero value exists for $t<0$, the system is noncausal. The graph-based support test gives the same conclusion as the symbolic support test: any nonzero negative-time component breaks causality.

example_content.example_prompt: Identify the negative-time support of $h(t)=4e^{-0.5t}u(t-2)-2u(-t+1)$ and classify causality.

explanation_blocks.text: Treat this as a support-triage task. The cue is the unit-step terms, so use the causality rule: a continuous-time LTI system is causal only if every nonzero part of $h(t)$ vanishes on $t<0$.

Split the expression into its two support contributors. For the first term, $u(t-2)=0$ for $t<2$, so $4e^{-0.5t}u(t-2)$ has support only for $t\ge 2$. For the second term, $u(-t+1)=1$ when $-t+1\ge 0$, i.e. $t\le 1$, so $-2u(-t+1)$ is active on the nonpositive-to-negative side.

Apply the strict negative-time test: intersect each support set with $t<0$. The first support $[2,\infty)$ has no negative-time overlap, but $(-\infty,1]$ contributes all negative times, so the combined impulse response is nonzero on $t<0$.
A quick sample verifies it. At $t=-1$, $h(-1)=4e^{0.5}u(-3)-2u(2)=0-2=-2\neq 0$. A nonzero negative-time value is enough to fail the causality prerequisite.
Conclusion: because $h(t)$ has nonzero negative-time support, the system is noncausal. If causality fails here, do not rely on pole-based stability conclusions until the support rule is satisfied.

sections.section_title: Verifying Causality Before Using Pole Locations

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+1}$, state the time-domain causality check flow before applying pole-location stability rules and show the consequence if $h(t)$ were found noncausal.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the sequence control requirement: this lesson always tests causality first, then only proceeds to pole-based BIBO rules. Start by finding a time-domain form of $h(t)$ and checking support before reading poles.
Invert $H(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+1}$ using the standard pair. With a causal ROC choice, $h(t)=\sin(t)u(t)$. This form is right-sided, so its support is $\{t: t\ge 0\}$.
Check the strict causality condition from this topic: $h(t)$ must satisfy $h(t)=0$ for all $t<0$. For $h(t)=\sin(t)u(t)$, the condition is satisfied, so the system is causal at this checkpoint.

Now the flow is explicit: causal result first, then pole-location interpretation. If this step had returned a noncausal form such as $h(t)=\sin(t)u(-t)$, we would stop here, report noncausal status, and defer any BIBO claim from pole locations because the prerequisite is violated.
Therefore, the example answer is: verify right-sided support from the inverse transform, accept the causality prerequisite, and only then run the next stability decision rule.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Verify causality of an LTI system by checking that its impulse response satisfies $h(t)=0 for all t<0 in the pole-based stability setting$.

sections.section_title: Checking $h(t)=0 for t<0 from an Impulse Response Formula$

prompt_blocks.text: Given $h(t)=2u(t)-3u(t-1)+u(-t-2)$, is the system causal or noncausal?

choice_blocks.text: Noncausal, because $u(-t-2)$ is nonzero for $t<-2$.
Causal, because every term contains a unit step and therefore vanishes for $t<0$.
Causal, because $u(-t-2)=0$ for every negative $t$.
Noncausal, because $u(t-1)$ creates negative-time support.
Causal, because the coefficients are finite and the response is bounded.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $u(-t-2)$ is active when $-t-2\ge 0$, so it is nonzero for $t\le -2$. That gives a negative-time interval where $h(t)\neq 0$, which violates the causality test $h(t)=0$ for all $t<0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $h(t)=4e^{-t}u(t)+u(-t+1)-2u(t-3)$, is the system causal or noncausal?

choice_blocks.text: Noncausal, because $u(-t+1)$ is nonzero for some $t<0$.
Causal, because the right-shifted term $u(t-3)$ makes the response one-sided.
Noncausal, because $4e^{-t}u(t)$ grows for $t<0$.
Causal, because $u(-t+1)$ only matters at $t=0$.
Causal, because the response decays for positive time.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because $u(-t+1)$ is nonzero for some $t<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $u(-t+1)$ is active when $-t+1\ge 0$, so it is nonzero for $t\le 1$. That includes negative-time values such as $t=-1$, where the impulse response is already nonzero, so the system is noncausal.

sections.section_title: Checking Causality from an Impulse Response Graph

image_slots.image_description: Graph of $h(t)$ versus t with clear $t$- and $h(t)$-axes, a short nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval around $t=-1.2$ to $t=-0.8$, and a right-sided exponential tail for $t\ge 0$; no other negative-time support.
Graph of $h(t)$ versus t with clear $t$- and $h(t)$-axes, a single impulse-like spike at $t=0$, a right-sided exponential tail for $t>0$, and zero response for all $t<0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the graph of $h(t)$ below to decide whether the system is causal or noncausal.

choice_blocks.text: Causal, because the graph has no nonzero support for $t<0$.
Noncausal, because the graph has a nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval.
Causal, because the left-side pulse is really on $t>0$ if the time axis is read backward.
Noncausal, because the right-sided exponential tail alone makes the system noncausal.
Causal, because isolated negative-time spikes do not count in the support test.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because the graph has a nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A continuous-time LTI system is causal only when $h(t)=0$ for every $t<0$. This graph has a nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval, so the impulse response is not zero for all $t<0$ and the system is noncausal.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the graph of $h(t)$ below to decide whether the system is causal or noncausal.

choice_blocks.text: Causal, because there is no nonzero support for $t<0$, and the spike at $t=0$ is allowed.
Noncausal, because any nonzero value at $t=0$ makes the system noncausal.
Noncausal, because the right-sided exponential tail means the system depends on future inputs.
Noncausal, because the graph is bilaterally supported.
Causal, because the spike at $t=0$ should be treated as negative-time support.

questions.correct_answer: Causal, because there is no nonzero support for $t<0$, and the spike at $t=0$ is allowed.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Causality depends only on whether $h(t)$ is zero for all $t<0$. This graph has no negative-time support, so the system is causal. A spike at $t=0$ does not violate the causality test.

prompt_blocks.text: Identify the negative-time support of $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t-2)+\frac{1}{2}\big(u(-t+1)-u(-t-4)\big)$ and classify causality.

choice_blocks.text: Causal; support on $[2,\infty)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-4,0)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,0)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,2]$.
Causal; support on $(-4,0)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The windowed difference $u(-t+1)-u(-t-4)$ is nonzero for $-4<t\le 1$, so it produces negative-time support on $(-4,0)$. Since $h(t)$ is nonzero for some $t<0$, the system is noncausal. The $e^{-t}u(t-2)$ term is right-sided and does not change that conclusion.

prompt_blocks.text: Identify the negative-time support of $h(t)=3u(t)-u(t-2)+\frac{3}{4}u(-t-4)$ and classify causality.

choice_blocks.text: Causal; support on $[0,\infty)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,-4]$.
Noncausal; support on $[-4,\infty)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,2]$.
Causal; support on $(-\infty,-4]$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $u(-t-4)$ is active when $t\le -4$, so the impulse response is nonzero on negative time. That alone makes the system noncausal. The right-sided terms $3u(t)$ and $-u(t-2)$ do not remove the left-sided support.

sections.section_title: Verifying Causality Before Using Pole Locations

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s+1)(s+4)}$, which step comes first before using pole locations to conclude BIBO stability?

choice_blocks.text: Verify causality from $h(t)$ first; if a noncausal term appears, stop before the pole test.
Check only the pole locations because rational transfer functions are always causal.
Conclude BIBO stable immediately because all poles are in the left half-plane.
Test BIBO stability first and infer causality from the result afterward.
Declare the system noncausal because the transfer function has a zero at $s=-2$.

questions.correct_answer: Verify causality from $h(t)$ first; if a noncausal term appears, stop before the pole test.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This lesson requires the time-domain causality check before any pole-location conclusion. Pole locations are only used after $h(t)$ has been verified to satisfy $h(t)=0$ for all $t<0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose the inverse transform gives $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)-3u(-t-1)$. What should you conclude before any pole-location stability check?

choice_blocks.text: Causal, because the $e^{-2t}u(t)$ term is right-sided and dominates.
Noncausal, because the $u(-t-1)$ term is nonzero for some $t<0$, so the pole test should not be used yet.
Stable, because the negative exponent guarantees BIBO stability.
Causal, because any unit-step term makes the response right-sided.
Noncausal only if the poles are in the right half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because the $u(-t-1)$ term is nonzero for some $t<0$, so the pole test should not be used yet.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Any nonzero negative-time term breaks causality. Since $u(-t-1)$ is active for $t\le -1$, the impulse response is noncausal, and this lesson says to stop before using pole locations.
